name: Botox for underarm sweat
lead: Botulinum toxin injections for underarm sweat place a neurotoxin into the skin of the armpit to reduce excessive sweating (axillary hyperhidrosis). The looks payoff is dry underarms: no sweat rings or visible damp patches on shirts, less yellowing and staining of clothing, and more freedom to wear fitted or light-coloured clothes. The toxin blocks release of acetylcholine from nerve endings, the signal that tells sweat glands to produce sweat.[1][2]

The American Academy of Dermatology describes botulinum toxin as FDA approved for hyperhidrosis, with most patients noticing less sweating within 7 to 10 days and results for the underarms or hands lasting about 3 to 10 months.[4] Wikipedia's hyperhidrosis article describes it as an option for severe underarm sweating that topical agents have not controlled, and lists injection pain as a drawback.[2]

On T Nation, members mention it as the option that worked after other measures failed; one reports no sweat for two years and gives a rough annual cost, and another asks about reported lab-animal findings on toxin spread.[5][6][7] Published trial material includes a small registered trial of botulinum toxin with suction-curettage.[3]
infobox: FDA approved for hyperhidrosis per AAD[4]
Prescription antiperspirants, topical glycopyrronium, oral anticholinergics, microwave thermolysis, surgery[2][4]

paras: Botulinum toxin type A cleaves proteins involved in nerve-ending signalling and so prevents acetylcholine release, producing temporary paralysis of muscle in its better-known cosmetic uses.[1] In hyperhidrosis the same blockade of nerve signals to the sweat glands reduces sweat output.[2] A dermatologist injects it, and the AAD notes that dermatologists buy it directly from the manufacturer and that choosing a board-certified dermatologist helps minimize risks.[4]

Wikipedia's hyperhidrosis article describes botulinum toxin as used for severe underarm sweating that topical treatments cannot manage, gives an effect duration of about 3 to 9 months depending on site, and attributes the first demonstration of a non-muscular use to Khalaf Bushara and colleagues in 1993.[2] Injection is painful, and ice is mentioned as one pain-reduction measure.[2]

Focal hyperhidrosis is estimated to affect as much as 2.8 percent of the US population, men and women equally, most commonly between ages 25 and 64, and 30 to 50 percent of affected people have a relative with it.[2] Wikipedia reports that over 80 percent of patients describe moderate to severe emotional effects, that researchers have called it a silent handicap, and that people may avoid handshakes or change shirts several times a day.[2]

For appearance, the practical goal is clothing that stays dry and unmarked. On T Nation, one 2006 poster says loose moisture-wicking shirts were the only thing that helped him, while a 2003 poster working in an office says soaked armpits are what he wants to avoid.[9][10]

Wikipedia lists clinical-strength aluminium-based antiperspirants as first-line, then oral anticholinergics such as glycopyrrolate and oxybutynin, topical glycopyrronium tosylate (FDA approved in 2018 for primary axillary hyperhidrosis), botulinum toxin, microwave thermolysis (miraDry), and surgical options including sweat gland removal and sympathectomy.[2] The AAD likewise lists prescription antiperspirants, glycopyrronium cloths, sofpironium gel, iontophoresis, a sweat-control patch, oral medicines and surgery, and says plans are individualized by type, location and preference.[4]

The AAD lists pain, bruising, headache, muscle soreness or weakness at the injection site and mild itching as the most common side effects, and says studies show the treatment can be safe and effective. It advises stopping aspirin, certain anti-inflammatory drugs and vitamin E before treatment to lower bruising risk.[4]

Wikipedia's botulinum toxin article reports that in 2008 the FDA warned the toxin can spread from the injection site, especially in children with cerebral palsy, and that boxed warnings were announced in 2009. It also notes the FDA approved Botox Cosmetic for glabellar lines in 2002.[1] The effects are temporary, so treatment is repeated.[4]

T Nation threads from 2008 to 2010 include a reply that Botox injections can stop underarm sweating, a member who says nothing worked until Botox and that the cost was about 500 dollars a year, and a thread titled 'Finally Got My Botox' where a reply explains that the thread concerns excessive underarm sweating specifically rather than sweating in general.[5][6][8] Another poster considering the injections cites lab-animal research that toxin can travel along neurons from the injection site and asks about it; those are the member's reading of studies, not clinical findings in people.[7]

A small registered trial (NCT01274611, 20 participants, started 2010) examined botulinum toxin together with suction-curettage for axillary hyperhidrosis; results are not posted in the registry record.[3] The AAD summary and Wikipedia's hyperhidrosis article describe the FDA approval for severe primary axillary hyperhidrosis and typical onset and duration figures, without trial-level numbers in the pages cited here.[2][4]

General reference sources list injection pain and the possibility of unintended spread of toxin effect to nearby muscles as recognised issues of botulinum toxin treatment.[1][2] The AAD lists bruising, soreness, muscle weakness at the site and itching as common effects.[4]

timeline.event: Richard Clark reports botulinum toxin for forehead wrinkles after a facelift complication.[1]
Khalaf Bushara and colleagues demonstrate a non-muscular use of botulinum toxin.[2]
FDA approves Botox Cosmetic for glabellar lines.[1]
Boxed warnings announced for botulinum toxin products after spread concerns.[1]
FDA approves topical glycopyrronium tosylate for primary axillary hyperhidrosis, an alternative to injections.[2]

lore.intro: Underarm Botox appears in T Nation threads on sweating and body odour, usually as a last-resort option after antiperspirants and clothing choices.[5][6][8]

claims.claim: Botox stops underarm sweating for long stretches.
claims.believers: One member says he had no sweat for two years after treatment; another says nothing worked until Botox.[6]
claims.experts: The AAD reports onset in 7 to 10 days and results lasting about 3 to 10 months.[4]

claims.claim: The toxin can travel to the brain.
claims.believers: A member considering underarm injections cites lab-animal research that the toxin can travel along neurons from the injection site.[7]
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports FDA warnings about spread of the toxin from injection sites to other muscles and boxed warnings since 2009.[1]

claims.claim: Loose, moisture-wicking clothing and treatments are the practical ways to hide sweat
claims.believers: A 2006 T Nation poster says the majority of his wardrobe is loose athletic shirts and that this was the only thing he found to help.[9]
claims.experts: The AAD describes individualized treatment plans that can include prescription antiperspirants, devices, oral medicines, injections or surgery.[4]

chain: Toxin blocks acetylcholine release at sweat-gland nerve endings
Underarm sweat output drops for months
Dry underarms, no visible sweat patches or shirt staining
angle.text: A clinician injects the underarm skin, and sweat production there falls for roughly 3 to 10 months. People use it so shirts stay dry and sweat marks do not show.

card.summary: Neurotoxin injections that switch off underarm sweat glands for months at a time, a clinician-delivered option with thin entry-specific research.
card.note: Effect is temporary and requires repeat injections.

quick.overview:
Botox for underarm sweat means injecting botulinum toxin into the armpit skin to reduce sweating. It is described in reference sources as an approved option for severe underarm sweating that topical products have not controlled.

The effect is reported to last about 3 to 9 months, after which injections are repeated.
quick.mechanism: The toxin blocks release of acetylcholine from nerve endings, so the nerves stop signalling sweat glands to produce sweat.
quick.risks: Injections can be painful. General botulinum toxin warnings include spread of effect to nearby muscles. The effect wears off and treatment is repeated.
